newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Hard-fought elections for Security Council seats.
newsitem.headline: Hard-fought elections for Security Council seats.

text.p: Kenya is virtually certain to be elected by the General Assembly on Monday to a two-year term on the Security Council beginning on Jan. 1, but seven countries were vying to fill four other council seats that become vacant at the end of the year.

India and Japan are in a particularly fierce contest for an Asian seat now held by Indonesia, while Australia, Portugal and Sweden are vying for two places reserved for members of the group known as West European and Others, currently filled by Germany and Italy.
Costa Rica and Bolivia were both seeking election to a Latin American and Caribbean seat to be vacated by Honduras.

Regional groups usually nominate a single candidate for each vacancy. This makes the results of secret balloting in the 185-nation General Assembly, where a two-thirds majority is required, a foregone conclusion.
Kenya is the unopposed candidate of the African group to succeed Botswana on the 15-nation council. But none of the other three regional groups has agreed on a candidate.
The council comprises five permanent members with the power of veto -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France -- and 10 non-permanent members who serve two years.
The non-permanent members whose terms expire at the end of 1997 are: Chile, Egypt, Guinea-Bissau, Poland and South Korea.
A working group has been discussing enlarging and reforming the council for nearly three years, but it has not yet decided how this should be done.

It is widely accepted that if any new permanent seats are created two of them should go to Germany and Japan in recognition of their status as economic superpowers and increasing involvement in such areas as peacekeeping.

Japan, which has already had seven turns on the council, most recently in 1992-93, was reported by diplomats to have engaged in particularly strong lobbying including use of its economic clout to beat out India for a non-permanent seat.

India, which has served on the council six times including in 1991-92, has wide support among the 112 members of the non-aligned group but could forfeit some backing because of its hold-out role in opposing a recently concluded Compehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty.

By contrast Australia, which has been on the Security Council four times, most recently in 1985-86, is likely to benefit from its lead role in shepherding the test ban treaty through the General Assembly last month. India's opposition to the treaty in the Geneva Disarmament Conference, which acts by consensus, helped block its adoption there.

Sweden, which was a council member in 1957-58 and 1975-76, is given the edge by some diplomats over Portugal for the other seat reserved for the West European and Others group, even though Portugal has served only once, in 1979-80.

Costa Rica, current chairman of the Group of 77 developing nations which now has 138 members, is in a tight race with Bolivia. Diplomats said Costa Rica, which has had only one term as a council member in 1974-75, and Bolivia, which served in 1964-65 and again in 1978-79, have agreed that whoever gets fewer votes on the first ballot will withdraw from the race.

Balloting in close contests can be protracted. But no one expects a repeat of what happened in October 1979 when a race between Cuba and Colombia to fill a Latin American seat required 155 ballots that stretched into the following January and ended with the election of Mexico as a compromise.
